title: Cloud Platforms for AI
summary: Production AI usually runs in the cloud, which offers on-demand compute, GPUs, storage, and managed ML services. The big three (AWS, GCP, Azure) each provide platforms like SageMaker or Vertex AI that handle training, deployment, and scaling. You do
content:
# Cloud Platforms for AI ##### The GPU that ran for eleven days A student spun up an AWS `p3.2xlarge` instance to fine-tune a model. Training finished in six hours. They downloaded the weights, closed the laptop, and moved on. Nobody stopped the instance. At roughly $3.06 an hour, it ran for eleven days before the billing alert they had never configured would have fired — except they had not configured one. The bill was **$807**. This is the most common cloud mistake in machine learning, and it is entirely preventable with two settings and one habit. GPU instances are expensive by the hour and invisible when idle, and cost awareness is not a footnote to cloud skills — it is a core part of them. ##### The three providers AWS, Google Cloud and Azure offer broadly equivalent capabilities with different strengths and terminology. | | AWS | GCP | Azure | |---|---|---|---| | Managed ML | **SageMaker** | **Vertex AI** | **Azure ML** | | Object storage | S3 | Cloud Storage (GCS) | Blob Storage | | Containers (serverless) | App Runner, Fargate | **Cloud Run** | Container Apps | | Kubernetes | EKS | GKE | AKS | | Serverless functions | Lambda | Cloud Functions | Functions | | Notebooks | SageMaker Studio | Colab Enterprise, Workbench | Azure ML Studio | | Foundation models | Bedrock | Vertex AI Model Garden | Azure OpenAI | The honest characterizations: **AWS** has the largest service catalogue and the most job postings, at the cost of complexity. **GCP** has the cleanest developer experience — Cloud Run in particular is the simplest path from container to public URL — plus strong TPU access and BigQuery. **Azure** dominates where organizations already run Microsoft, and hosts Azure OpenAI, which many enterprises prefer for compliance reasons. For learning, **the concepts transfer completely**. Object storage is object storage; a container service is a container service. Learn one properly and the second takes days. ##### Compute and GPU instances Choosing the right instance is the largest cost lever available. | Type | Example (AWS) | Approx $/hour | Use for | |---|---|---|---| | CPU general | `t3.medium` | 0.04 | Development, small API serving | | CPU compute | `c6i.2xlarge` | 0.34 | Feature engineering, classical ML | | GPU entry | `g4dn.xlarge` (T4, 16 GB) | 0.53 | Inference, small fine-tuning | | GPU mid | `g5.xlarge` (A10G, 24 GB) | 1.01 | Most fine-tuning | | GPU high | `p3.2xlarge` (V100, 16 GB) | 3.06 | Large training | | GPU top | `p4d.24xlarge` (8×A100) | 32.77 | Foundation model training | Two rules that follow directly: **Do not use a GPU for inference on classical models.** A scikit-learn or XGBoost model runs faster on CPU than the GPU transfer overhead costs. GPUs are for deep learning training and, sometimes, deep learning inference at volume. **Right-size, then scale.** Develop on a small instance, profile, and move up only when you have measured the bottleneck. Renting an A100 to debug a data loader is a common and expensive habit. Three pricing models change the arithmetic substantially: **On-demand** — full price, available immediately, no commitment. **Spot / preemptible** — 60–90% cheaper, but the provider can reclaim the instance with two minutes' notice. **Excellent for training with checkpointing**, unusable for serving. **Reserved / committed use** — 30–60% cheaper for a one- or three-year commitment. Right for steady production load. Spot instances deserve emphasis because they change what is affordable. A training run that costs $32/hour on-demand costs perhaps $10 on spot — and if your training loop checkpoints every N steps and resumes, interruption is an inconvenience rather than a loss. ##### Storage Object storage — S3, GCS, Blob — is where your datasets and model artifacts belong. It is cheap, effectively unlimited, and durable. ```python import boto3 from pathlib import Path s3 = boto3.client("s3") s3.upload_file("models/fraud_v1.joblib", "my-ml-bucket", "models/fraud/v1/model.joblib") s3.download_file("my-ml-bucket", "data/train.parquet", "/tmp/train.parquet") # Presigned URL — temporary access without exposing credentials url = s3.generate_presigned_url( "get_object", Params={"Bucket": "my-ml-bucket", "Key": "models/fraud/v1/model.joblib"}, ExpiresIn=3600, ) ``` Storage classes matter for cost. Standard is roughly $0.023/GB/month; infrequent-access tiers are around half that; archival tiers are a tenth but with retrieval delays. **Lifecycle rules** move data automatically: ```json { "Rules": [{ "Id": "archive-old-training-data", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": "data/raw/"}, "Transitions": [ {"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"}, {"Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR"} ] }] } ``` The cost trap that catches people is **egress**. Storage is cheap; *downloading* data out of the cloud costs roughly $0.09/GB. Moving a 500 GB dataset out is $45, and doing it repeatedly during development adds up. Keep compute in the same region as your data, and avoid cross-region transfers. ##### Deploying a container This is the most practical skill in the article, and the serverless container services make it genuinely simple. **Google Cloud Run** is the shortest path — one command from a local image to a public HTTPS URL with autoscaling: ```bash gcloud run deploy fraud-api \ --source . \ --region asia-south1 \ --memory 2Gi --cpu 2 \ --min-instances 0 \ --max-instances 10 \ --concurrency 40 \ --timeout 60 \ --set-secrets "API_KEY=fraud-api-key:latest" \ --allow-unauthenticated ``` `--min-instances 0` means **scale to zero** — you pay nothing when there is no traffic. That is the decisive feature for a portfolio project or a low-traffic internal service: a deployed API that costs nothing when idle. The trade-off is a **cold start** of a few seconds on the first request after idling, which you mitigate with `--min-instances 1` when latency matters. **AWS App Runner** is the equivalent: ```bash aws apprunner create-service \ --service-name fraud-api \ --source-configuration '{ "ImageRepository": { "ImageIdentifier": "123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/fraud-api:v1", "ImageRepositoryType": "ECR", "ImageConfiguration": {"Port": "8000"} }}' \ --instance-configuration '{"Cpu": "1 vCPU", "Memory": "2 GB"}' ``` **Managed ML endpoints** — SageMaker, Vertex AI — add ML-specific features: A/B traffic splitting between model versions, built-in autoscaling on inference metrics, model monitoring and data capture. They cost more and lock you in more, but for production ML they remove real work: ```python from sagemaker.sklearn.model import SKLearnModel model = SKLearnModel( model_data="s3://my-bucket/models/fraud/v1/model.tar.gz", role=role, entry_point="inference.py", framework_version="1.2-1", ) predictor = model.deploy( initial_instance_count=1, instance_type="ml.m5.large", endpoint_name="fraud-detector-v1", ) ``` The decision, framed practically: **use a serverless container service unless you need what managed ML endpoints provide.** For a single model behind an API, Cloud Run or App Runner is simpler, cheaper and portable. Reach for SageMaker or Vertex AI when you need traffic splitting for canary deploys, automated model monitoring, or a managed training-to-deployment pipeline. ##### Cost management The discipline that prevents the $807 bill. **Set budget alerts before you create anything.** This is the single most important step, and it takes two minutes: ```bash gcloud billing budgets create \ --billing-account=$ACCOUNT \ --display-name="ML learning budget" \ --budget-amount=50USD \ --threshold-rule=percent=50 \ --threshold-rule=percent=90 \ --threshold-rule=percent=100 ``` **Tag every resource** so you can attribute spend: ```bash aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-1234567890 \ --tags Key=Project,Value=fraud-detection Key=Owner,Value=ananya Key=Env,Value=dev ``` **Automate shutdown.** A scheduled job that stops development instances outside working hours cuts their cost by roughly 70%: ```python import boto3 from datetime import datetime def stop_dev_instances(event, context): """Lambda on a schedule — stops tagged dev instances nightly.""" ec2 = boto3.client("ec2") reservations = ec2.describe_instances(Filters=[ {"Name": "tag:Env", "Values": ["dev"]}, {"Name": "instance-state-name", "Values": ["running"]}, ])["Reservations"] ids = [i["InstanceId"] for r in reservations for i in r["Instances"]] if ids: ec2.stop_instances(InstanceIds=ids) return {"stopped": ids} ``` The estimation habit worth building — do this arithmetic *before* provisioning: ```text Fine-tuning job: g5.xlarge spot @ ~$0.35/hr × 8 hours = $2.80 S3 storage, 50 GB × $0.023/GB/month = $1.15 Egress, 2 GB model download × $0.09/GB = $0.18 ------ $4.13 Serving (Cloud Run, scale to zero): 100k requests/month × 200ms × 2 vCPU ≈ $3.50 Idle cost = $0.00 ``` Free tiers are genuinely useful for learning: **Google Colab** provides free GPUs (with session limits), AWS and GCP offer credits for new accounts, and Hugging Face Spaces hosts demos free on CPU. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Model ready to deploy] --> B{Traffic pattern?} B -->|intermittent / demo| C[Cloud Run / App Runner
min-instances 0
pays nothing idle] B -->|steady production| D{Need A/B, monitoring,
managed pipeline?} D -->|no| E[Container service
min-instances 1+] D -->|yes| F[SageMaker / Vertex AI
managed endpoint] B -->|batch only| G[Scheduled job
Batch / Cloud Run Jobs] C & E & F & G --> H[Budget alert
+ resource tags
+ auto-shutdown] ``` ##### Security essentials Four practices, all of which matter from the first deployment. **Never hard-code credentials.** Use IAM roles for services and OIDC federation for CI — GitHub Actions can assume an AWS role without any stored key: ```yaml - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-deploy aws-region: ap-south-1 # no secret key anywhere ``` **Least privilege.** A model-serving container needs read access to one S3 prefix, not `AmazonS3FullAccess`. **Secrets in a secret manager** — AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager — injected at runtime, never baked into images. **Data residency.** Choose your region deliberately. Indian personal data under the DPDP Act, or European data under GDPR, may need to stay in a specific jurisdiction — `asia-south1` (Mumbai) or `ap-south-1` rather than a US region. ##### Common mistakes - **Leaving GPU instances running** — the $807 lesson. - **No budget alerts** configured before provisioning. - **GPU instances for classical ML inference**, where CPU is faster and cheaper. - **On-demand pricing for interruptible training** where spot would cost a third. - **Repeated egress** during development, quietly accumulating charges. - **Untagged resources**, making spend impossible to attribute. - **Over-provisioning** rather than measuring and right-sizing. - **Hard-coded credentials** instead of IAM roles and OIDC. - **Overly permissive IAM policies.** - **Ignoring data residency** requirements when choosing a region. - **Managed ML endpoints for a single simple model**, paying for features you do not use. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **deploy your Dockerized model API to a cloud service** and call it over the internet. Cloud Run with `--min-instances 0` is the recommended route — you get a public HTTPS URL in one command, and the idle cost is genuinely zero, so leaving it running costs nothing. **Set a budget alert first**, before you create anything. The mini project is a **complete AI app deployed to the cloud** with proper storage and a public endpoint, documented with **estimated costs**. That cost documentation is the part most people skip and the part that demonstrates engineering maturity: a README section stating "approximately $4/month at 50k requests, scaling to zero when idle" shows you thought about operating the system, not just shipping it. For the assignment, **compare the three providers' AI offerings and describe when to use a managed ML service**. Keep the comparison honest — the capabilities are broadly equivalent and the differences are ecosystem, developer experience and existing organizational commitments. For the managed-service question, give the decision rule: use a plain container service for a single model behind an API, and reach for SageMaker or Vertex AI when you need traffic splitting for safe rollouts, built-in model monitoring, or managed training pipelines — and note the trade-off in cost and portability. ##### Key takeaways - Set budget alerts and tag resources before provisioning anything; idle GPU instances are the most common and most expensive cloud mistake. - Match instance type to workload — CPU for classical ML, GPU only for deep learning — and use spot pricing for checkpointed training runs. - Object storage with lifecycle rules is cheap; egress is not, so keep compute in the same region as your data. - Serverless container services with scale-to-zero give you a free-when-idle public endpoint in one command — reach for managed ML endpoints only when you need A/B splitting or built-in monitoring. - Use IAM roles and OIDC rather than stored credentials, apply least privilege, and choose your region for data residency as well as latency.
